messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ade was, by all accounts, a prodigy. At nineteen, he had already secured a junior UX designer position at a competitive tech startup in the city, a role he fulfilled with a quiet, intense focus that impressed his older colleagues. The work was his life, a world of logic, empathy, and clean lines that felt orderly and predictable. That world had shattered six months ago. It began, as he recalled with a sickening clarity, with a simple message on a professional networking site. An admirer of his portfolio, another designer, wanted to connect. Ade, eager to build his professional circle, had responded with what he now saw as a catastrophic friendliness. He had been open, encouraging, and had shared a few details about his current projects. This, he was now certain, was his mistake. The event happened, he believed, because of the way he acted.

The messages from the man became a daily, then hourly, deluge. They shifted from professional admiration to unnervingly personal questions, then to declarations of affection, and finally, to anger when Ade tried to set boundaries. The digital siege escalated into a physical one. One evening, as Ade left his office building, the man was standing across the street, just watching. The sight of him—no longer an avatar but a physical presence—sent a current of ice through Ade’s veins. After that, he was everywhere: on the same subway car during Ade’s morning commute, standing near the coffee shop where he got his lunch. The world, which had once felt full of opportunity, had shrunk to a landscape of potential ambush points. Though a restraining order eventually made the man disappear, the feeling of being watched did not.

Now, Ade lives in the aftermath. The core belief that the world is a dangerous place has become the organizing principle of his life. His commute to the office is a gauntlet of threat assessment. He stands on the subway platform with his back pressed against a pillar, constantly scanning the faces in the crowd, his phone clutched in his hand not for distraction but as a potential weapon or a way to call for help. At work, he has chosen a desk in the far corner of the open-plan office, a position that allows him to see everyone who enters the room. He can’t tolerate anyone walking behind him; the soft footfalls of a colleague approaching with a question make him flinch, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has to be especially careful, he tells himself, because you never know what can happen next. This constant vigilance is exhausting. He finds it impossible to sink into the deep focus his design work requires, his mind perpetually divided between the pixels on his screen and the subtle shifts of movement in his peripheral vision.

His professional life, once a source of pride, is now a source of terror. User-testing sessions, which require him to sit in a small room with a stranger and observe them, have become unbearable. The last time he tried to lead one, he found himself unable to focus on the user’s interaction with the prototype, his attention locked instead on the person’s hands, their tone of voice, their proximity to the door. He began making excuses to pass these tasks to others, a move that did not go unnoticed by his manager. His social life has evaporated. Invitations from friends are met with vague refusals. The idea of being in a loud bar or a crowded restaurant, environments he can’t control or easily exit, feels like willingly stepping into a trap. He spends his evenings alone in his apartment, checking the locks on his door three, four, sometimes five times before he can even attempt to relax. It was after receiving a formal warning about his declining performance at work that Ade finally sought help. The thought of losing the one part of his identity he had left—the talented young designer—was more terrifying than the prospect of sitting in a room and finally telling someone the full story. He came to therapy not with a grand hope of reclaiming his old life, but with a desperate, simple plea: to one day be able to sit with his back to the door and not feel like he is about to die.
